articles.title_zh: Expert Reacts to First U.S.-Russia-China Summit: Pageantry, Policy and Nuclear Diplomacy - Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation
articles.source: Center for Arms Control and Non-Proliferation
articles.content_orig:
For the first time in history, the leaders of the United States, Russia and China — the world’s three largest nuclear powers — have sat down together for a formal trilateral summit. Coming after the expiration of New START in February left the two largest nuclear arsenals without legally binding limits, President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration committing to dialogue on nuclear risk reduction and non-proliferation. Host Cameron Lopez sits down with Senior Policy Director John Erath — a 30-year State Department veteran and former National Security Council official — to unpack what the meeting actually accomplished and what it means for global security.
820 1st Street NE, Suite LL-180 Washington, D.C. 20002 Phone: 202.546.0795

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.content_orig:
It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.”
Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.”
It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.”
Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.”
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.”
Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke.
In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959.
Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway.
Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling.
“Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.
Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.”
Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy.
“The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.”
But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity.
Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said.
Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II.
But it is Ukraine’s plucky defiance of Putin's invasion that underscores how today’s Middle Powers have more agency. At the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney urged third countries to work together on trade, security and technology in order to shape the rules and resist economic coercion. “Middle powers must act together because if you are not at the table, you are on the menu,” Carney said.

articles.title_orig: S&P 500 and Dow enter correction, Nasdaq wipes out 2026 gain as Anthropic leads AI sell-off: Live updates
articles.title_zh: S&P 500 and Dow enter correction, Nasdaq wipes out 2026 gain as Anthropic leads AI sell-off: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Stocks were slammed on Friday, closing out a brutal week for markets as the much-hyped Anthropic IPO caused investors to take profits on the artificial intelligence-led rally rather than revive it. The Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year, and the S&P 500 entered correction territory alongside the Dow Jones Industrial Average .
The tech-heavy Nasdaq shed 3.6% and was down 1% year to date. The broad market S&P 500 traded down 2.2%, while the blue-chip Dow fell 352 points, or 0.7%. Both the S&P 500 and Dow were more than 10% below their closing records.
Anthropic lost 12%, giving back most of its 17% jump in its Nasdaq debut Thursday and pressuring the broader AI trade. Chipmakers Advanced Micro Devices and Nvidia slid 11% and more than 7%, respectively. Micron Technology dropped more than 12%.
Those declines in tech built on the losses seen in Thursday's horrid session, where the major averages each losing more than 2%, and the Dow closing below the key 50,000 level for the first time since June.
"This is not just a valuation-driven correction. It's becoming broader," said Massimo Santicchia, head of U.S. equities at Procyon. "Right now, it's definitely risk-off."
The losses are alarming investors who were hopeful that Nvidia's earnings and Anthropic's IPO would revive enthusiasm for the AI trade. Now, the market looks to be on the cusp of a true capitulation after getting roiled in recent weeks with a series of negative headlines. Signs of moderation in the capital expenditures splurge, Democratic wins in the 2026 midterms and Jensen Huang's ouster at Nvidia all raised questions about the future of the AI buildout.
On top of that, the potential for more interest rate hikes from the Federal Reserve is spooking traders as well.
Investors hid out in defensive areas of the market, with retailers such as Walmart and Costco as well as others like Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble seeing gains. Walmart gained almost 3%, while Costco added nearly 2%. Johnson & Johnson and Procter & Gamble each rose more than 1%.
"The stock market is going through an AI repricing, reflecting an environment of slowing data center buildouts, reduced funding sources for AI-related projects and a slower trajectory of technology-related earnings growth," said Richard Saperstein, chief investment officer at Treasury Partners.
For the week, the Dow has fallen 6%, putting it on pace for its worst weekly performance since April 2025 in the wake of President Donald Trump's sweeping tariffs announcement . The S&P 500 has decreased 7%, while the Nasdaq is down about 8%, with both also headed for their largest one-week pullbacks in more than a year.
President Donald Trump said on Friday that he wants to stop U.S. companies from building data centers in other countries.
"We're going to fight very hard for the data centers," Trump said at a White House press conference. He added that companies would face tremendous penalties for building data centers abroad. "We want them to build it here."
He added that he is concerned about U.S. companies building in China instead. "We're not allowing that to happen," he said.
— Kevin Breuninger and Davis Giangiulio
The VIX volatility index , a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, rose another 13% intraday Friday to 32.27, after jumping as much as 16% Thursday, according to FactSet data.
The VIX, a gauge of skittishness on Wall Street, has now risen for six of the past seven days. The index hasn't closed above 30 since late March.
Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook expressed caution about the dangers posed by inflation, saying Friday that if the central bank doesn't act now it risks having to do more later.
"Inflation has been above target for more than five and a half years, and every additional day poses greater risk that price- and wage-setters will adjust their inflation expectations upward," Cook said in remarks delivered in Chile.
"Furthermore, waiting longer to implement rate increases risks getting behind the curve," she added. "If we fall behind, additional and larger rate increases may be required later to catch up, which could increase stress on our financial system and have unnecessarily damaging effects on American households."
Cook was one of only two FOMC members who voted against the pause. Markets strongly expect the committee to approve a quarter percentage point hike at the Dec. 8-9 meeting.
The tech selling intensified in late-morning trading, with the sector down more than 5% on the day. That decline pushed its week-to-date losses to 10.5% as of 11:57 a.m. ET. That would be tech's biggest one-week drop since April 4, 2025, when the Trump administration announced massive tariffs on imported products.
The Nasdaq Composite dropped Friday, turning negative for 2026, as even Anthropic's IPO and Nvidia's earnings failed to revive the artificial intelligence trade. The tech-heavy index was last lower by 2.6% for the trading session, falling slightly on the year.
Bitcoin slid more than 4% with the broader market, falling below the $60,000 level for the first time since July.
The flagship cryptocurrency was last trading at $59,554.95 and is now heading for a retest its July low of $57,737.35.
Ether fell 6% to $1,650.79, its lowest level since July 2.
The outlook for consumers improved in November as expectations for inflation eased, according to a University of Michigan survey Friday.
The survey's headline sentiment index rose to 51.5, up 7.3% from a month ago and exactly in line with the Dow Jones consensus estimate.
Inflation expectations at the one-year horizon declined sharply, down to 3.7%, which was a full percentage point below a month ago and well below the mid-month November reading of 4.3%. This was the lowest reading since March. The five-year outlook slipped to 3.3%.
"Despite the softening in inflation expectations, consumers continue to report overwhelmingly that inflation—rather than unemployment—will cause greater hardship for consumers in the next one or two years," survey director Joanne Hsu said.
The recent pressure seen in technology stocks as well as the S&P 500 may not be over yet, according to James Reilly, senior markets economist at Capital Economics.
"The success of Anthropic's IPO yesterday as other AI-related stocks tumbled highlights how different parts of the AI ecosystem no longer move as one," he wrote in a Friday note. "We think the falls in tech stocks and the S&P 500 have further to run — and how this plays out within the stock market will depend on what is driving these falls."
Reilly believes the S&P 500 index should fall to 6,500 by the end of next year. The index closed at 7,175.83 on Thursday.
The three major averages were trading in the red on Friday morning.
The Nasdaq Composite declined 1.3% just after 9:30 a.m. ET, while the S&P 500 moved down 0.5%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 48 points, or 0.1%.
Anthropic made its historic Wall Street debut on Thursday. But one research firm is taken a cautious stance on the stock.
Seaport Research initiated coverage of the artificial intelligence stock with a neutral rating.
"Anthropic is an incredible company, but it is also asking for an incredible leap of faith by investors," analyst Jay Goldberg said in a note. "We think the company will need time to grow into its valuation and answer some very big questions about its growth trajectory. We are not negative on the company, but we are cautious."
CNBC Pro subscribers can read more here .
Check out CNBC's live blog here to read more about the stocks making premarket moves.
— Deena Zaidi, Darla Mercado and Fred Imbert
The CBOE Volatility Index (VIX) was trading above 30 on Friday morning as the selling pressure on U.S. equity futures ramped up.
The index, also known as Wall Street's "fear gauge," was last at 30.99, reaching its highest level since March.

articles.title_orig: When Nazis were held responsible for war crimes
articles.title_zh: When Nazis were held responsible for war crimes
articles.content_orig:
Holocaust historian Bill Tinglin, on Thursday during a panel discussion in Bethage on the Nuremberg trials, said a lesson learned from the tribunals is people must be held accountable, even if "they have uniforms or they’re doing things that they said they were led by their government to do." Credit: Debbie Egan-Chin
One by one, the accused Nazi war criminals who hadn't died by suicide or other means lined up in a Nuremberg, Germany, courtroom 81 years ago Friday to face what had previously seemed almost beyond belief: justice.
The start of the Nuremberg Trials on Nov. 20, 1945 , their legacy of successfully bringing the powerful to justice for committing atrocities in the name of hate, and ways to make sure something like the Holocaust is never repeated, were the topics of a panel discussion Thursday at the Museum of American Armor in Bethpage .
"We must hold people accountable [even if] they have uniforms or they’re doing things that they said they were led by their government to do," said Dr. Bill Tinglin, a Holocaust historian who sat on the panel. "That’s how the Nuremberg [defendants] were held accountable."
Several dozen people turned out for the event, which was organized by the Garden City-based law firm Rosenberg, Calica, Birney, Liebman & Ross. In addition to Tinglin, the panel included Mindy Perlmutter, the executive director of the Jewish Community Relations Council , Gloria Sesso, who chairs the Long Island Council for Social Studies, retired U.S. Army Col. Jason Halloren and Joshua Liebman, a partner with the host law firm.
Time has not erased the antisemitism that fueled the rise of Adolf Hitler and the Nazi defendants at Nuremberg, according to the panel speakers.
The Anti-Defamation League put the number of antisemitic incidents nationwide in 2024 and 2025 combined at roughly 16,000.
"My grandfather would be forced to say that things are starting to look frighteningly familiar, when compared to the streets of Vienna before the Holocaust," said museum spokesperson Gary Lewi in an email to Newsday after the discussion, citing "today’s events that are happening out there with swastikas on synagogues."
A recent example occurred in Lawrence. On Nov. 10, the Nassau County Police Department arrested and charged a Brooklyn man after he allegedly drew a swastika on a Jewish community center in the village.
Sesso, the social studies education expert, said a major outcome of the Nuremberg trials was the documentation of the crimes of the Holocaust, allowing its history to be taught accurately.
Halloren, the retired Army officer, who is the Museum of American Armor’s senior trustee, said the trials set an international legal foundation "for holding people accountable."
"All the things that led up to [atrocities like the Holocaust] — the creating a perception that a certain population ... is evil — to allow that to go on is criminal in nature," Halloren said.
Sam Kmack covers the Town of Islip for Newsday. He is a graduate of the University of Southern California and previously worked as a city watchdog reporter in the Phoenix metro area, as well as an investigative journalist at the Arizona Center for Investigative Reporting.

articles.title_orig: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
articles.title_zh: China attackers deployed AI agents that autonomously found and exploited a 0-day to take over a university server
articles.content_orig:
'Agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction,' Amazon CISO said
Suspected Chinese spies deployed AI agents which worked autonomously to find a zero-day in an open source application and then abuse the flaw to break into university networks, gaining full control of a server, according to Amazon CISO CJ Moses.
The China-linked attacker used Cairn, an open source, penetration-testing framework that has become increasingly popular with cybercriminals who use the AI tool to carry out multi-stage intrusions with no human assistance .
In this case, the agents found and exploited a zero-day MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging AI application. Amazon notified the project's maintainers of the vulnerability, and they released a fix and a security advisory .
On September 10, Amazon's Threat Intelligence Team found a server with a publicly hosted instance of Cairn that provided visibility into the campaign targeting universities in East Asia, outside Mainland China, Moses said in a Friday report shared with The Register .
The campaign occurred over a period of 48 hours beginning on September 8, and the prompts were written in Simplified Chinese, with timestamps in executed scripts configured to China Standard Time.
Before the AI agents found and exploited the zero day, however, they tried to break into another university’s Redis server over about 16 hours and 148 sequential actions, including abusing Redis's replication feature to load unauthorized code, escaping its scripting sandbox, writing to its configuration files, and corrupting its memory.
None of these were successful, and when those actions failed, the agents also attempted a Log4Shell injection against a different service, a server-side request forgery (SSRF) attack against a vulnerability in a co-located Qdrant instance, and several credential sprays against PostgreSQL, SSH, and other tools.
Meanwhile, a separate operation running for more than 6 hours targeted a university GPU server with another credential-spray attack, compiling a list of 80 real user names found across the school’s public websites, academic papers and other documents.
"Neither operation succeeded, yet together they show that the agents kept adapting for nearly a full day without human direction," Moses wrote.
Then the AI agents found the zero-day path traversal vulnerability in MONAI Label, and this time they were able to gain access to the server.
"The agents identified the application's framework, mapped its API endpoints, and found an upload endpoint with a filename parameter," Moses wrote. They tested that parameter for path traversal, and the parameter was vulnerable. In about 11 minutes, the agents went from mapping the application’s API to arbitrarily writing files on the server."
Later, the agents abused the same flaw to execute a Python reverse shell running as root.
In another session, after the agents discovered the zero-day, the human operator provided them with a proxy that tunneled into a second university network, and connected to a server running the same vulnerable code.
Amazon's discovery follows an earlier report by Gambit Security's threat intelligence team that also documented a Chinese operator using Cairn to carry out at least 105 attacks, and managing to compromise, "to varying degrees," at least 27 companies.
This campaign also occurred in September. In addition to Cairn, the attacker used two other open source AI harnesses to steal credit card records and other sensitive data from a Fortune 500 hospitality company, a major US airline, a large private US industrial supplies distributor, and a US online fashion retailer, and other companies.
"Together, these cases show that this autonomous AI agent framework is being adopted in both espionage and criminal operations," Moses wrote. ®

articles.title_orig: Britain Announces Brexit Reset Deal at E.U. Summit: What to Know
articles.title_zh: Britain Announces Brexit Reset Deal at E.U. Summit: What to Know
articles.content_orig:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

articles.title_orig: ‘Buyers are out for blood’: With home sales at a record low, buyers are calling the shots
articles.title_zh: ‘Buyers are out for blood’: With home sales at a record low, buyers are calling the shots
articles.content_orig:
Two new reports on the housing market show activity slowing even more, after a September spike in mortgage rates sent it into a deep freeze.
Pending home sales in October dropped 4.7% month-over-month and were down 16.7% from October of last year, according to the National Association of Realtors. This is the lowest level in the index's 25-year history.
Analysts had been looking for a much smaller decline, likely because mortgage rates pulled back slightly in October, only to rise sharply again last week. The average rate on the 30-year fixed started October at 7.54% according to Mortgage News Daily and ended the month at 7.27%.
The pending count is based on signed contracts — people out shopping and signing deals during the month. It is therefore an indicator of future closed sales.
"Two consecutive months of record-low pending contracts point to very sluggish fourth-quarter home sales closings, and annual existing-home sales could be the lowest since the mid-1990s," said Lawrence Yun, NAR's chief economist in a release.
Regionally, sales were down across the nation with the sharpest drops in the South, which is usually busiest for sales and the West which is most expensive.
Another report released Wednesday showed gains in home construction in October but raised a red flag going forward. Single-family housing starts rose 4% from September, according to the U.S. Census, but were down 3.2% year over year. Building permits, an indicator of future construction, dropped 8.7% for the month and were down 12.9% from October 2025. That is the lowest level for permits since May 2020, the start of the Covid-19 pandemic.
"Builders are dealing with a litany of obstacles to selling homes, whether it's rising costs of land, labor, and materials, high financing costs, or weak buyer demand," wrote Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com. "This month's data shows them slowing down activity at the top of their funnel, which will result in slower months of starts and completions later on."
The construction report follows a bleak reading on homebuilder sentiment , which fell to the lowest level in 14 years in November, on the monthly index from the National Association of Home Builders. Builders cited multiple challenges, including higher mortgage rates, higher costs for energy, materials and labor, as well as weaker consumer confidence.

articles.title_orig: Four men guilty of assaulting woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.title_zh: Four men guilty of assaulting woman drugged and advertised for sex by husband
articles.content_orig:
LONDON — Four British men were found guilty Thursday of multiple sexual crimes, including rape, against a woman whose then-husband drugged and advertised her for sex online, in a case that raised widespread comparisons to that of Gisèle Pelicot in France.
Joanne Young, who waived her right to anonymity as Pelicot had, spoke of her “relief” at the jury verdict and urged other women who have experienced anything similar to go to authorities in the knowledge that they “can be believed and understood.”
“Knowing what has happened to me without my knowledge or consent has been incredibly difficult to process, and this abuse has cost me my life as I knew it,” she said outside Winchester Crown Court in southern England. “The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.”
The 49-year-old mother of three spoke after the jury found the four men, whose ages range from 32 to 62, guilty of abusing her at her home in Swindon after being recruited on the internet.
Her ex-husband, Philip Young, had previously pleaded guilty to dozens of offenses including 11 counts of rape and 11 of administering a substance with intent.
Norman Macksoni, 48, was found guilty of one charge of rape. Richard Wilkins, 62, was found guilty of one count of rape and one of assault by penetration. Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, was convicted of sexual assault by penetration and sexual touching while Mohammed Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape.
Justice Pushpinder Saini said the four men faced “significant” prison sentences and praised Joanne Young for her “amazing bravery throughout these proceedings.”
The court heard that over a 13-year period, Philip Young, who served as a locally-elected official for the Conservative Party in Swindon between 2007 and 2010, drugged and raped his wife and invited other men on websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.
Joanne Young said her case raised “serious questions” over how the law deals with consent and urged the government to look into the issue to better protect women.
“Consent has to come from the person themselves, no one should be able to give it on your behalf, and no one should be able to rely on someone else’s word that you agreed,” she said. “At no point did anyone ask me for my consent.”
James Foster, specialist prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service, said the men found guilty “chose to commit unspeakable acts of abuse against Joanne Young without bothering to check if she was consenting.”
Domestic abuse charity Refuge said the guilty verdicts represented “long overdue justice” but “cannot undo the devastating abuse inflicted upon” Joanne Young.
“Echoing the case of Gisèle Pelicot in 2024, the atrocities committed against Joanne by Philip Young and multiple other men are a clear reminder that, in the powerful words of Gisèle, shame must change sides,” it said.
In December 2024, Pelicot’s ex-husband, Dominique Pelicot, and 50 other men were convicted of sexually assaulting her between 2011 and 2020 while she was under chemical submission. He was sentenced to 20 years in prison, while the other defendants received sentences ranging from three to 15 years.
The shocking case of Pelicot and her decision to waive her anonymity and speak publicly prompted a reckoning over rape culture in France and beyond.
Philip Young’s abuse came to light in July 2024, when the local Wiltshire Police force received information that an account on the free mobile messaging and livestreaming app Kik linked to him had uploaded three extreme bestiality images to the platform. Full searches of his devices then identified five videos showing Joanne incapacitated and tied to the bed at their shared home address as well as chat threads which showed that Young had shared intimate images of Joanne online without her knowledge.
“It is hard to put into words the depth of Young’s exploitation and abuse of Jo,” said senior investigating officer detective superintendent Geoff Smith. “Young put her health at risk through deliberately drugging her without her knowledge and inviting strangers to rape her, depriving her of autonomy over her own body.”
Joanne Young said she now never feels completely safe, but said that with the support of her loved ones she is “working hard to rebuild my life.”

articles.title_orig: Donald Trump seeks Ukraine peace deal before January
articles.title_zh: Donald Trump seeks Ukraine peace deal before January
articles.content_orig:
US envoy also says he believes Moscow is ‘comfortable’ with a guarantee; Russia attacks Kyiv bridges after Putin vows response for Crimea bridge attack. What we know on day 1,731
US envoy Jared Kushner has said Donald Trump is open to extending Ukraine a security guarantee similar to Nato’s mutual defence clause , but stressed that Washington has to protect its interests too. French president Emmanuel Macron meanwhile urged Kyiv’s allies to “reopen the question” of Ukraine becoming a member of the military alliance. Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, told a press conference in Germany: “From America’s perspective, giving an Article 5-like security guarantee is a really, really big deal. And I think that that’s something that President Trump is open to, but obviously it has to be in America’s interest to do that. We also have to make sure that it’s part of a broader security package.”
Kushner’s comments came after Ukraine’s allies gathered for a summit of the “coalition of the willing” in Berlin with Volodymyr Zelenskyy to emphasise support for Kyiv nearly five years since Russia’s 2022 invasion, and to push for a European role in future peace negotiations. Kushner added on Thursday that “we’ve gotten the Russians comfortable with that concept, where any security guarantee for Ukraine would be based on Article 5 ”. He noted that went with Moscow’s intention to “not have another war” when this conflict was over, while acknowledging “scepticism” over the position.
Macron called on Ukraine’s allies to do the “maximum” to deliver the air defence systems it needed, as well as looking again at Ukraine joining Nato . “Faced with the maximalist nature of the Russian position, I believe we need to reopen the question of Ukraine’s accession to Nato,” the French president said in Berlin. “Everyone who has the capacity to provide the means to defend and protect Ukrainian citizens must do so now,” he said, adding the priority was to deploy anti-missile systems and interceptors.
Vladimir Putin said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea would be “painful” , after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week. The Russian president claimed he had considered agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed, report Dan Sabbagh and Jakub Krupa .
On Friday, after Putin’s threat, a Russian ballistic missile attack hit three ⁠bridges on Kyiv’s Dnipro River and killed three people , the city’s mayor said, in the ⁠biggest strikes on routes ⁠connecting ​the left and right banks of Ukraine’s capital since the war began. The missiles hit the ⁠ Podilsko-Voskresenskyi bridge crossing as well as the Darnytskyi and Pivdennyi bridges , Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram, resulting in closure or ⁠traffic restrictions. About ‌15 people were injured, he added. The strikes also caused fires ‌and damaged critical infrastructure and buildings. In the north-eastern city of Kharkiv, a Russian drone damaged a hospital, wounding four people, mayor Igor Terekhov said. In ‌Russian-controlled Luhansk, three ⁠people ​were ⁠killed ⁠in ​a Ukrainian ‌attack, said Russian-installed ‌authorities of ​the ⁠eastern Ukrainian ​region.
The summit of the coalition of the willing on Thursday was co-hosted by the leaders of Germany, Britain and France shortly after unprecedented three-way talks in China between Trump, Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping. China, Russia and the US said after their talks they had agreed to a peace statement, but the declaration made no mention of the war in Ukraine. The European coalition’s meeting in Berlin expressed indignation at the trilateral’s cosy optics, reports Rebecca Bailey . “Mr Putin is not our friend and ⁠will never be,” the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said in a rejoinder to Trump.
German chancellor Friedrich Merz said he expected new Ukraine peace talks would “take place soon” , with Europe now set to have a seat at the table alongside the US, Russia and Ukraine. Merz, speaking in Berlin, did not give a date and added that “we are looking for locations on neutral ground”, naming the United Arab Emirates as a possible location. British prime minister Andy Burnham said: “I hope that message is heard very clearly in Moscow. For as long as it takes, we will be there at the side of Ukraine and we will not falter.”
A wave of daytime Russian strikes on Kyiv on Thursday killed one person and damaged the historic Saint Volodymyr Cathedral as well as the embassies of Austria and the Netherlands. “Russia has been terrorising Kyiv with drones all day ... At least four people are known to be injured so far, and one person was killed,” prime minister Sergiy Koretsky said.

articles.title_orig: Saudi Arabia attacks Yemen's Houthis and intercepts more missiles and drones, and other Mideast news
articles.title_zh: Saudi Arabia attacks Yemen's Houthis and intercepts more missiles and drones, and other Mideast news
articles.content_orig:
Yemen’s Houthis and the Saudi Arabia-led coalition have exchanged threats to bomb key ports in the latest round of escalation between the warring parties.
⁠On Friday, the Houthis threatened to attack Saudi Arabia’s Red ⁠⁠Sea ports if Saudi-led coalition forces follow through on threats to strike the Houthi-held Yemeni ⁠⁠port city of Hodeidah. The Iran-backed armed group also warned airlines to stay out of Saudi airspace because it was planning ⁠new strikes within hours.
The threats come a day after the Houthis struck the tallest skyscraper in Riyadh , raising fears of further escalation in a conflict that has caused a humanitarian crisis in Yemen and severe disruption in ⁠⁠Saudi Arabia, in parallel with the wider US-led war against Iran.
On Friday, the Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s internationally recognised government urged civilians ⁠⁠to evacuate areas of Hodeidah port for their safety, without providing further details.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree then responded on X, saying that Jeddah port and all Saudi ports on the Red Sea coast would become “targets” if the coalition carried out its threat to strike Hodeidah port.
“We warn all employees, workers, and those in the vicinity of [Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea] ports to evacuate them immediately and stay away. We also urge all shipping companies to immediately evacuate their ships from these ports,” he said.
Airlines should avoid Saudi airspace “because it will be the scene of our operations in the coming hours”, Saree said, making an exception for airspace near the Muslim holy cities of Mecca and Medina. He also said the group would target a power station at Shuqaiq in southern Saudi Arabia.
Shortly afterwards, the Saudi-led coalition said on X that it had begun a “targeted operation” against Houthi assets it claimed are being used to target civilians in Saudi Arabia and Yemen.
“We targeted operational capabilities at Hodeidah port that were used in smuggling operations and the transport of weapons and ballistic missiles,” spokesman Turki al-Malki wrote, adding that operations were “ongoing” in Sanaa, Saada and Taiz governorates.
In Sanaa, which is the Houthi-held Yemeni capital, the coalition said it targeted the Houthis’ ballistic missile and drone capabilities.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa, said there are “warnings from both sides and both sides seem to be delivering on their promise to step up their aerial assault”.
He said a number of Saudi coalition air strikes and drones targeted the city on Friday morning. The targets included what the coalition claimed were military sites and workshops used to produce ballistic missiles and drones.
Meanwhile, the Houthis – also known as Ansar Allah, Arabic for Supporters of God – launched a series of their own attacks and issued warnings that they would attack other sites, he said.
“Both sides seem to be stepping up their attacks. These are the heaviest air strikes that we have witnessed since the conflict began. And both sides seem to carry a very serious tone in delivering on their promise to target [sites including] energy infrastructure and airports,” Mawry added.
Fighting is raging in other parts of Yemen , with the Houthis advancing on the government’s de facto capital of Aden in recent weeks. Government forces are now preparing for the defence of the coastal city – their last real stronghold.
The Houthis also continue to besiege the government-held city of Taiz, north of Aden. That city has now been cut off from Aden, and residents have complained of shortages of water and fuel.

articles.title_orig: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.title_zh: Poland condemns Russian 'provocation' after three airspace violations
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

For the past decade, success in quantum computing has been measured through research breakthroughs, investment, and technical milestones. This is beginning to change. Across industries, organizations are focusing on viable quantum solutions, shifting the conversation from theoretical potential towards practical application.
This acceleration presents a strategic challenge for governments. As commercial markets increasingly focus on real-world use cases, there is a risk that governments’ ability to adopt quantum technologies will fail to keep pace. Businesses can experiment with emerging technologies in quick iterations, but governments must navigate long procurement cycles and stringent internet security requirements.
This challenge is compounded by the need for governments to identify priority use cases and communicate them to the commercial market at an appropriate level of sensitivity. Without sufficient visibility into these requirements, systems may be developed in ways that do not align with, or are not appropriate for, government use cases.
Executive Vice President, Capabilities at IQT.
Keeping pace is also made harder by the fact that quantum technologies can’t be developed in isolation. Progress relies on international supply chains, access to specialist infrastructure and facilities, and a highly skilled workforce capable of developing and deploying these technologies.
As quantum’s breakthrough moment approaches, competitive advantage will depend not simply on who develops or invests in the technology first, but on who has the capabilities in place to operationalize it and make it useful.
Financial services is one industry already experimenting with how quantum computing could be incorporated into its technology stacks. For example, NatWest joined Digital Catapult’s Quantum Technology Access Programme to explore quantum computing for fraud detection, with the aim to move beyond concept to practical application.
The same can be said of the cybersecurity industry. The prospect of Q-day, a hypothetical future moment when quantum computers become powerful enough to break standard public-key encryption, is influencing strategies. Likewise, the arrival of post-quantum cryptography means organizations can begin protecting information against future quantum attacks before powerful quantum computers exist.

Microsoft is accelerating its quantum-safe security roadmap to replace encryption standards vulnerable to future quantum computers. Progress like this will be critical to ensuring the US and other nations are not left exposed if Q-day arrives, with governments playing an important role in setting standards and supporting the widespread implementation of quantum-safe security across critical systems.
The defense sector is also putting quantum technologies into practice. Quantum sensing solutions, which provide highly precise positioning, navigation, and timing when satellite navigation is denied or jammed, have moved to testing and early deployment stages. Examples include atomic clocks, magnetometers, and quantum inertial sensors.
Taken together, these developments demonstrate an important shift, where technologies that have spent years in research and development are now moving towards testing and early deployment.
But unlike commercial organizations, public-sector adoption must navigate procurement, security, regulation, and integration with existing systems. The risk is that commercial capabilities develop faster than governments build the institutional capacity to absorb them. By the time a technology is mature enough to deploy at scale, beginning the preparedness process will already be too late. And right now, the timeline to get prepared is only a couple of years.
Earlier this year, the UK government announced £2 billion to establish the UK as a world leader in quantum, including programs to accelerate the development, manufacturing, and procurement of quantum computers. The challenge now is ensuring that funding translates into operational readiness, which is a distinction every government, not just the UK, will need to manage. As quantum computing matures and increasingly works alongside traditional systems, governments can’t afford to wait until commercially viable capabilities materialize before asking where they might be useful.
This also matters beyond the public sector. Governments act as both investors and early customers. By identifying priority use cases and, where appropriate, communicating those requirements to industry, governments can give companies greater clarity on the capabilities they will need. Procurement and testing can then help companies validate those solutions against real-world challenges and accelerate adoption. In a nascent industry like quantum, speed matters. Companies that scale early can gain an outsized role in shaping technical standards, informing regulatory frameworks, and influencing how the wider market develops.
Governments need to anticipate national security implications and opportunities, identify which applications matter most, provide training for their workforce, and create mechanisms to bring commercially developed technology into government quickly. They must also guide responsible development and adoption by establishing safeguards and governance frameworks.
Beyond preparedness, quantum is a global technology, increasingly dictated by physical resources, supply chains, and human talent. Governments must also be building resilient supply chains into their quantum strategies, while businesses need to understand how policy decisions could shape the technologies, suppliers and skills available to them.
In the UK, 85% of quantum companies import elements of their supply chain. At the same time, quantum supply chains are at risk due to heavy reliance on sole suppliers for key components, such as cryogenic refrigerators. These dependences create potential points of vulnerability. A country may possess world-leading quantum research but be constrained by physical resources and materials.
Addressing this will require investment in critical areas such as cryogenics and lasers. Governments can help create clearer demand by supporting testing, procurement, and adoption. As the market scales and technology requirements become clearer, manufacturers will have greater incentive to invest in the capacity needed to build more resilient supply chains.
Then there is talent. The UK Quantum Skills Taskforce has highlighted that the UK is at a “pivot point”, emphasizing that having the skills to develop and adopt quantum technologies will be critical to future growth. Developing the technology requires deep scientific expertise but deploying it requires a much broader workforce capable of engineering systems, developing software, and integrating quantum into existing organizations.
With specialist talent limited and in high demand, countries must consider how they can attract and retain these skills. Universities are critical to this pipeline, but governments and industry must ensure that expertise can move beyond academi

articles.title_orig: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.title_zh: ILO and China reaffirm commitment to South-South cooperation for decent work and social justice
articles.content_orig:
12th Joint Committee Meeting reviews progress and explores new opportunities to strengthen cooperation on employment, skills, social protection and emerging challenges in the world of work.
GENEVA (ILO News) – The International Labour Organization (ILO) and China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security (MOHRSS) have reaffirmed their commitment to advancing decent work and social justice through South-South cooperation, with a focus on emerging labour-market challenges and partnerships across the Global South.
The commitment was highlighted at the 12th Joint Committee Meeting on ILO–China Cooperation, held in Geneva on 20 November 2026. The meeting reviewed progress since the previous Joint Committee Meeting in 2021 and explored opportunities to deepen cooperation.
The discussions took place against a backdrop of rapid technological change, persistent labour-market inequalities and the need to accelerate progress towards the Sustainable Development Goals.
Participants underscored the importance of translating development cooperation into practical improvements focusing on areas of longstanding cooperation including employment opportunities, skills and social protection.
Since 2021, China-supported ILO initiatives have contributed to strengthening institutional capacity, policy exchange and knowledge sharing, particularly across countries in the Asia-Pacific region.
Cooperation in skills development has supported training institutions and responses to growing demand for digital, green and industry-relevant skills. Employment initiatives have promoted high-quality and full employment, stronger public employment services, entrepreneurship and regional policy dialogue. In social protection, cooperation has supported efforts to expand coverage and improve service delivery, including through digital transformation.
Participants emphasized the importance of building on these achievements, sharing good practices and strengthening national institutions to ensure sustainable results.
Looking ahead, discussions explored how South-South cooperation could help countries navigate changes in the world of work, particularly those associated with artificial intelligence and the platform economy.
Participants considered opportunities to harness technological innovation for productivity and employment while addressing potential risks for workers and enterprises. They also highlighted the importance of connecting country-level initiatives with regional and global policy dialogue to broaden the impact of development cooperation.
The meeting further considered the role of the ILO–China partnership within wider development frameworks including the Global Development Initiative (GDI) and the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). China’s presidency of the BRICs in 2027 will also offer an important opportunity to advance cooperation on various world of work issues.
China has been a member of the ILO since its founding and has developed a longstanding partnership with the Organization. The ILO–China cooperation framework encompasses employment promotion, skills development, social protection, occupational safety and health, and South-South cooperation. Through technical cooperation, policy dialogue and knowledge exchange, the partnership supports countries in advancing decent work and meeting the Sustainable Development Goals.

articles.title_orig: Russian missiles and drone hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Russian missiles and drone hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow
Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland, according to officials, during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries.
Poland accused Moscow of “provocation” after the strikes in the south-east area of the Nato country.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, said it was “one of the largest attacks” since the full-scale Russian invasion in 2022, with at least eight people killed and nearly 30 injured in Ukraine.
“The Russians spread this attack across many cities and regions of Ukraine. Absolutely all the targets were ordinary civilian infrastructure – things that literally sustain people’s lives,” he said.
Zelenskyy said Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, went ahead with the strike after “weak meetings” with the US president, Donald Trump, and China’s Xi Jinping, and his “failure to attempt to somehow redraw the world”.
The Ukrainian president added: “Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror.”
Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, confirmed three violations of Polish airspace, with no injuries reported.
He said he believed it was “not accidental” that the incident took place on the same day as major western military exercises involving troops from 11 countries in the “coalition of the willing”, including the UK.
The incidents were reported in Nowy Lipowiec, Mołodycz and Rudnik nad Sanem in south-eastern Poland, between 30 miles (50km) and 60 miles from Nowa Dęba, where the exercises are taking place.
Poland’s prime minister called the incident “an intentional provocation” by Russia.
Donald Tusk said he had spoken with Nato’s secretary general, Mark Rutte – who will visit Warsaw on Saturday – who agreed with him that “it does not seem to be a coincidence” that the attack took place on the night before the drills.
“It clearly shows … that coming months … will certainly pose great challenges for all of us,” he said.
“Today’s incident shows clearer than ever before why Poland must participate in decisions on Ukraine’s future,” he added, arguing that Warsaw has a “better understanding” of the threat posed by Russia.
Rutte said on X: “Spoke with @donaldtusk about the grave violations of Polish airspace overnight. NATO jets were scrambled in response. We stand in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend.
“This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine. I condemn Russia’s attacks as well as its ongoing war. We continue to stand united as Allies and will continue to support Ukraine.”
​The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who is in Poland for the exercises, described the incursion as “very serious” in a post on X, adding: “The impact of Russia’s illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries. The UK stands in solidarity with our allies.”
Maj Gen Ireneusz Nowak, commander of the operational command of the Polish armed forces, said as many as 11 objects had been identified as posing a danger to Polish airspace.
He also highlighted the unprecedented scale of the overnight attack on Ukraine, saying Russia used seven bombers and fired 26 Kalibr cruise missiles, 72 Kh-101 cruise missiles and more than 500 drones.
Air traffic control at Rzeszów-Jasionka airport – an international passenger hub and major transit point for military aid to Ukraine – was briefly evacuated overnight, for the first time since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine.
After the incidents, Tusk summoned army and security service chiefs to an emergency meeting to discuss the situation.
Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said the latest violations “demonstrate the threats posed by Russian aggression to the whole of Europe and the transatlantic community”.
He added: “While Moscow tries to initiate discussions about the ‘new security architecture of Europe’, Russian missiles and drones directly undermine the existing security order in Europe. The first step toward strengthening it would probably be to cease such attacks.”
Polish authorities repeatedly warned in recent months against potential security incidents as they feared an escalation in Russia’s war against Ukraine.
In July, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile fell in Poland’s Lublin region after veering off course during a nightly Russian attack on Ukraine.
In September last year, more than 20 Russian drones crossed into Polish airspace, with Tusk warning that the country was “closer to military conflict than at any time since the second world war”.
In November 2022, a Russian missile Kh-55 crashed near Bydgoszcz, more than 300 miles from Ukraine’s territory, but was only discovered in early 2023.

China’s crude oil imports from the Persian Gulf surged by 42.4% in October from September, to the highest level since the Iran war began, as supply via the Strait of Hormuz rebounded and Gulf producers slashed prices for their crude to attract buyers amid record-high freight rates.
China imported 19.7 million tons of crude oil from the Persian Gulf producers, excluding Iran, in October, a 42.4% jump from the previous month, per calculations by the South China Morning Post based on Chinese customs data released on Friday.
October was the fourth consecutive month in which Chinese crude oil imports from the Gulf countries increased from the previous month, according to the data.
Gulf producers shipped almost half of total Chinese term supplies last month, at a level approaching the pre-war volumes, the estimates by the South China Morning Post showed.
The surge in Chinese imports from the Gulf coincided with the recovery of crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz.
Additionally, Gulf producers reduced the prices of their crude grades loading for Asia as Hormuz flows rebounded and pressured down Middle Eastern crude benchmarks.
Rising supply from the Middle East has weakened both the Dubai and Murban prices. At the end October, the prices of physical Middle East crude slumped as flows from the region recovered and reached pre-war levels on some days.
Lower prices for December are expected to continue attracting buying interest in China, especially amid the slide in international crude oil prices.
Saudi oil giant Aramco earlier this month slashed the price for its flagship Arab Light crude for Asia for loading in December by $2 per barrel, to a discount of $6.50 per barrel to the Oman/Dubai average. This is the steepest discount for Saudi crude to the Middle East’s benchmark since May 2020 during the COVID pandemic.

articles.title_orig: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.title_zh: Ex-GM CEO on Mary Barra succession planning: 'It's going to be tough'
articles.content_orig:
Former General Motors CEO and Chairman Dan Akerson doesn't mince words when asked about the challenges the automaker faces in finding a successor for GM CEO Mary Barra : "It's going to be tough."
He should know. The 78-year-old businessman and U.S. Navy veteran helped with his own succession planning and recommended to GM's board in 2013 that Barra replace him as CEO. She has held the top job since Jan. 15, 2014.
Akerson said Barra will be hard to replace, citing her success and prominence as the first female CEO of any major automaker and the ongoing challenges facing the automotive industry, such as artificial intelligence , vehicle digitalization, and the rise of China and autonomous vehicles.
"It's going to be very, very dynamic," Akerson told CNBC during a phone interview. "It's going to be a big change."
Akerson declined to discuss potential internal candidates such as GM Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson , CFO Paul Jacobson or President Mark Reuss, but he said the eventual successor needs to be dynamic and, if from the outside, "adaptable."
His comments to CNBC follow a Wall Street Journal report on Tuesday that GM is working with an executive search firm to identify possible outside candidates to succeed Barra, in addition to internal prospects. GM declined to comment on the report or Barra's succession.
Akerson, who came to GM as an outsider from The Carlyle Group in 2010, said selecting an outside candidate might be risky if there are already executives within the organization who have similar leadership and technical expertise.
"Is there anybody in the organization that has that background that you know better day to day over a period of time? You may be taking a risk by bringing in an outsider," he said.
The prospect of an outsider leading GM would be unusual in the auto industry, where major automakers have generally promoted internal CEO candidates, apart from periods of exceptional disruption such as the Great Recession.
Stellantis , BMW , Toyota Motor , Nissan Motor and Hyundai Motor have all appointed internal executives to their CEO positions in recent years.
Barra has said several times that her successor and her longevity in the role would be determined by the board.
A notable influence is likely Hewlett Packard veteran Patricia Russo, GM's longest-serving board member who has been on the board since 2009 and leads its CEO succession planning as independent lead director.
GM's CEO succession planning is done "at least annually," according to the company's yearly proxy filing. That process includes Barra providing the board "with recommendations for, and evaluations of, potential CEO successors and discusses developmental plans for these successors," according to the filing.
That is followed by board members engaging "with CEO candidates and senior management talent at Board and committee meetings and other forums to enable directors to personally assess candidates."
When Akerson was preparing to retire, Barra was among a pool of four candidates — two longtime GM employees and two relative newcomers — who were finalists for CEO in 2013, he said.
Akerson said he put the finalists through an extended evaluation, asking how they viewed GM's strengths and weaknesses, how they would organize the company, and their willingness to work together, potentially with other CEO candidates who didn't get the job.
Akerson said the final decision to appoint Barra was done at a day-and-a-half-long board meeting in Washington. The candidate field was narrowed to Barra and former GM executive Dan Ammann , an ex-Wall Street banker who was GM's CFO before leaving the automaker's Cruise unit, reportedly over a disagreement in strategy with Barra, in 2021.
"Mary's very deserving of all the accolades she's received," Akerson said. "She's done a terrific job."
Barra has been leading the automaker for nearly 13 years, which makes her the longest-serving CEO of the automaker since Alfred Sloan retired after a 23-year career as CEO in 1946.
Akerson said he believes that, like he did, Barra will have major influence in picking her successor. He described that dynamic as integral to continuing her legacy leading the automaker.
"This is important. I think if she doesn't pick the right person, in four or five years from now and things are back in the trough, that will tarnish her history. But I think she'll pick the right one," he said.

articles.content_orig:
Payment services were unaffected, the companies said.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks and blamed the outage on a "software bug." The company said Thursday that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week" regarding the third-party provider data breach.
Mastercard also reported on Thursday that one of its third-party providers was hacked, while Visa said earlier this week that it was aware that one of its third-party providers experienced a data breach.
"They are associated with an incident involving a third-party service provider in Asia Pacific," Visa said in its statement. "Visa’s systems were not involved and were not impacted. No payments data such as card numbers were affected."
"We were recently informed of an incident at a third-party provider that resulted in the exposure of [a] limited amount of email addresses – non-payments information – from a small subset of cardholders enrolled in a specific benefit program," Mastercard said in its statement Thursday.
"There is no impact to the Mastercard payment network or the ability for people to use their cards," Mastercard further said. "At this time, the exposure has been contained, and our teams are working with the provider to support the impacted cardholders as needed."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: Watch: Trump to hold press conference after meeting with Xi and Putin
articles.title_zh: Watch: Trump to hold press conference after meeting with Xi and Putin
articles.content_orig:
In a pool photograph distributed by the Russian state agency Sputnik, Russia's President Vladimir Putin, China's President Xi Jinping and President Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting at Kylin Villa on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen, in China's southern Guangdong province, on Thursday. Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
President Trump is set to hold a White House press conference today at noon, following his return to Washington after a four-day trip to Asia , where he sat down for a rare three-way meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump did not formally take questions while in China at the end of his trip, though it's typically expected on presidential foreign trips. Putin did hold a press conference before leaving the country.
Watch the 12 p.m. ET news conference live:
The U.S. president said he will be discussing the historic meetings in China as well as trade agreements reached during the earlier part of the trip in the Philippines, where he arrived for the tail end of a summit with South Asian leaders.
Trump, Xi and Putin, who command the world's largest nuclear arsenals, gathered at a lakeside resort in Shenzhen, China, where they sat around a large round wooden table to discuss nuclear proliferation, Iran and global relations.
While the displays of power were prominent, the talks offered few signs that either Xi or Putin was prepared to make significant concessions to Trump.
"The trip enabled the president to bask in the glow of great power amity after a really bruising election outcome here at home," Suzanne Maloney, vice president and director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, said of Trump. "He wanted the optics of this direct engagement with Presidents Xi and Putin as a sort of validation of his own standing as a historical figure. And I think the photo op provided that."
Foreign trips are often largely about the pomp and circumstance involved in meetings between heads of state. Among other special events, Trump's arrival in China, for example, included a military flyover and young dancers.
But the events are also extensively choreographed, with aides working months in advance to lock down agreements and commitments that the leaders can point to as evidence of a successful trip. That did not appear to be a main objective for this visit.
For Xi, he was able to boast of China's global leadership by bringing together the world's greatest nuclear powers to discuss global challenges.
For Putin, the meeting allowed a chance to reestablish Russia as a great geopolitical power on par with China and the U.S.
And for Trump, it's a chance to turn the page and demonstrate his ongoing power at a time when he's been weakened domestically after the devastating midterm elections.
In his opening remarks alongside Xi and Putin, Trump said the three leaders were making history and that they had a responsibility to the rest of the world to maintain open and respectful dialogue.
"Too often, past leaders avoided talking to nations with whom they had disagreements. And we feel the opposite," Trump said. "No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about it. No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement and speech."
But while the kind words and pats on the back were prevalent, the lack of deliverables was also noteworthy.
It has raised questions about Trump's approach to foreign policy.
Trump has spent much of the last few years trying to replace the postwar rules-based order, ripping up traditional alliances in favor of a more personal approach to diplomacy. He prefers to work out deals personally with the world's superpowers.
But the visit may be demonstrating that access does not always produce results.
Xi and Putin have their own strategic objectives, which are not going to change because they're friendly with Trump. As Maloney put it, they also have to calculate whether agreements reached with Trump can survive domestic scrutiny or a change of administration in the coming years.
"I think both Putin and Xi recognized that President Trump's time is beginning to wane," Maloney said, "that his command of U.S. politics is also beginning to wane, and they're going to be looking to who and what may be coming next."
