articles.title_orig: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.title_zh: ‘The deal is done’: EU, UK agree to reset relations 10 years after Brexit
articles.content_orig:
The European Union has struck a deal on three policy areas with the United Kingdom in a move seen as the start of a reset of relations a decade after the Brexit vote.
After a summit in Brussels on Friday, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s office said negotiations have concluded and a reset ⁠deal has been sealed.
“This is a good day for Britain. This is a good day for Europe, and people across Europe and across the United Kingdom will get real benefit,” Burnham had told EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa at the start of the talks.
Downing Street said ‌both sides agreed timelines for implementing a youth mobility scheme, a sanitary and phytosanitary agreement, ⁠and a link ⁠between their emissions trading systems. Details are due ⁠to be published ⁠in a ⁠joint statement.
A UK government spokesperson told Al Jazeera: “The deal is done. Negotiations have concluded. Now both sides will work towards implementation.
“As with all international agreements, there is a legal process in each respective country which will now take place,” the spokesperson added. “And talks will continue on some areas.”
Burnham said the deals could add 0.5 percent to Britain’s economy.
The arrangement to reduce controls on the movement of animals, plants and related products between the UK and EU is worth an estimated 5.1 billion pounds ($6.7bn) to the British economy.
The agreement linking emissions trading systems will exempt British and EU goods, such as steel, from each other’s border carbon levies.
The youth mobility scheme will allow 100,000 young Europeans to live and work in the UK for up to three years, and vice versa.
Despite the agreements, months or years of negotiations lie ahead for a deeper reset in relations to take effect.
Burnham has previously told the British public all options should be on the table for future relations, including rejoining the now-27-nation EU.
However, he has stressed that reversing Brexit is just one possible outcome and far from imminent.
That possibility and the agreements sealed so far will incur anger from the significant section of the British public that remains eurosceptic.
Nigel Farage, leader of the populist right-wing Reform UK party, called Burnham “naive” following the news of the agreements.
The EU has used this moment to “strong-arm the British prime minister”, he claimed. “It’s the same old game, and he’s fallen for it out of sheer inexperience,” Farage wrote on social media.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang Scandal: Timeline That Led To His Resignation—And Potential Comeback
articles.content_orig:
Ted Glover is a former senior executive at several large multinational companies.
When an executive leaves suddenly, people watch to see whose calls still get returned. If they believe the old boss might be back in the foreseeable future, they have a reason to wait him out. At Nvidia , where Jensen Huang famously had dozens of direct reports, that ambiguity could reach deep into the business. Bill Ackman thinks Nvidia’s board made a mistake by saying it does not intend to reinstate Huang. I think that statement was one of the more defensible things the board did.
Ackman’s criticism of the original decision deserves a hearing. On Nov. 8, Nvidia announced an independent inquiry and expressed confidence in Huang. On Nov. 11, according to its SEC filing, the board accepted his resignation, effective immediately, and announced his departure the next day. Ackman argues that the directors moved too quickly. Chairman Harvey Jones says Huang resigned voluntarily after disclosing conduct inconsistent with company standards. The board has offered shareholders limited detail about what changed. The speed warrants scrutiny, although the public timeline alone cannot tell us what the directors knew or when they learned it.
But the question of whether the board handled Huang’s departure properly is different from the question of what should happen next. Once he was out, the directors could give interim CEO Colette Kress clear authority or leave employees, customers and prospective successors wondering whether Huang would soon return. Ackman sees the board’s rejection of reinstatement as another failure. A serious and highly qualified candidate for the permanent job might see it as a reason to accept the assignment.
When I ran large subsidiaries of major corporations, I would have found it impossible to imagine managing anything close to 60 direct reports. Bloomberg reported roughly that number at Nvidia. Huang’s extraordinary span gave him direct information and influence across the enterprise. Nvidia’s achievements offer a powerful defense of his approach, but they also reveal a succession problem. Access to one exceptional founder by so many direct reports is not an organizational structure that can easily be handed to someone else. Executives accustomed to relying on Huang for decisions almost certainly had fewer opportunities to exercise independent judgment.
The strongest case for Huang is not sentimental. He helped build one of the most consequential companies in modern technology, and his strategic and technical instincts may be unusually difficult to replace. But irreplaceability is a dangerous principle on which to govern a public corporation. The talents that made him an extraordinary founder do not necessarily make him the right leader during a prolonged investigation, legal uncertainty and a wholesale transition in authority.
Kress, who remains chief financial officer while serving as interim CEO, must keep the company moving. The permanent successor will face a different task: determining where authority belongs and making the new arrangement durable. I would allow roughly a year after that person takes charge before judging the transition. Reporting lines can change overnight; confidence in independent decision-making, customer relationships and accountability cannot.
Meanwhile, there is a practical reason to keep Huang away from day-to-day operations. A shareholder derivative lawsuit has named him alongside numerous directors and executives. Investigations and possible additional legal proceedings create uncertainty about the demands on his time; no one can responsibly predict their ultimate scope or outcome. But even intermittent diversions could be consequential at a company whose decision-making has depended so heavily on one person. An adverse finding after reinstatement could force a second abrupt transition. Berkeley law professor Stavros Gadinis has warned that reinstating Huang before the investigation concludes could expose directors to fiduciary risk.
Nvidia is not a distressed company desperately searching for a rescuer. On Nov. 17, it reported quarterly revenue of approximately $115.8 billion, more than double the year-earlier figure. Strong results do not prove the transition will succeed: most of that performance reflects work undertaken before Huang’s departure. They do, however, underscore what is at stake. The board’s task is to protect an exceptionally successful business from a leadership struggle that could unsettle it. Jones has reiterated that the board does not intend to reinstate Huang, and the company has engaged Heidrick & Struggles to help find a permanent CEO.
That stance need not mean throwing away Huang’s expertise forever. If the investigations end favorably, and if the new CEO wants his help, Huang might advise on a particular technical question or customer relationship under clearly defined terms. A board role or limited consulting arrangement might eventually be considered, subject to governance and conflict concerns. Even a return as CEO need not be metaphysically impossible if a successor fails and the circumstances change. But none of those possibilities should become a standing invitation to undermine the person now in charge.
Consider the alternative: a year after the permanent CEO arrives, Nvidia continues to prosper. Customers remain loyal, the leadership team has earned confidence, and executives are making decisions within their own authority. Bringing Huang back then could have more downside than upside, reviving uncertainty and displacing a system that had proved itself. If the transition falters, the board will retain options. What it cannot afford is to deny a successor the opportunity to succeed in the first place.
The board cannot undo the uncertainty surrounding Huang’s departure. But it can prevent that uncertainty from paralyzing Nvidia’s future. Giving a successor the authority to succeed, while preserving the option of drawing on Huang’s extraordinary talents later, is not a repudiation of his legacy. It may be the best way to protect it.

Join 100K+ fans and never miss breaking news, fan theories, trailers and exclusive content.
Grand Theft Auto 6 ( GTA 6 ) is what everyone’s playing right now, and one detail that we’re noticing is that the story starts off pretty slow. Once you complete Chapter 1, the game finally puts you in the shoes of Lucia as you try to recover your situation in Port Gellhorn. Early into the story, you’ll unlock Moses Watkins’ garage in Port Gellhorn, and you’ll finally be able to register a personal vehicle.

Stolen cars for Moses are the steadiest money, about $1,000 or more each.

@RockstarGames https://t.co/t2YWHlHHNw
You can only register vehicles without anti-theft GPS trackers at Moses’ workshop, and your first registration with him is completely free, so you’ll want to find the best vehicle to register. Once you register a vehicle, you can summon it anytime through the Scooter Bros app. Very cool mechanic, Rockstar Games .
The Emperor Sultan is one of the easiest cars to find in Port Gellhorn. This four-door sedan is a good overall car for all activities you’ll encounter in Chapter 2. And even if you don’t find one, you can earn Moses’ personal Emperor Sultan directly by completing his Port Gellhorn vehicle drop-off requests, registering it for just $1,600. It has good cornering, four-seat capacity, and generous trunk space, making it great for storing weapons, outfits, and any items you find.
In fourth place is the Dinka Chavos XS. It has a 497 road rating, 5.2 top speed, and 5.7 acceleration. The handling is great on both roads and light dirt paths. While it lacks the sheer muscle of the Dominator or Phoenix, it has a low-profile look, solid trunk storage, and can be found in the nearby area south of Port Gellhorn called Capri.
While not technically a car, the Nagasaki SFB 1000 is the best getaway vehicle you can register in Chapter 2. You can also find this in the nearby posh area of Capri. This sport motorcycle will get you through thick traffic and in tight spaces where cars just don’t fit. Just remember that riding two wheels trades away trunk storage and collision protection, making it the best for solo recon and quick escapes.
If you want classic GTA style paired with heavy V8 punch, the Imponte ’77 Phoenix is the car for you. The best part about it is that you can find it in Port Gellhorn itself, just south of the La Cascara Motel. With rear-wheel-drive muscle tuning, this retro coupe will zoom down highways and has plenty of visual customization options at local mod shops. Its vintage build keeps it free of modern anti-theft trackers, making it a great pick for your free initial registration.
Taking the top spot for best performance and style, the Vapid Firebug Dominator is a great modern muscle vehicle. You’ll easily outrun standard patrol cruisers and anything else Chapter 2 throws at you. It is a guaranteed spawn at the La Cascara Motel in Port Gellhorn, and you can bring it to Moses for a quick respray.
Before driving any boosted vehicle in Port Gellhorn, pull out Lucia’s phone and scan it with the WAiNK app to verify that the security readout shows no tracker installed. Use the Slim Jim Moses provides to slip past door locks quietly without triggering alarms or drawing unwanted police heat.
Keep in mind that Moses will reject vehicles stolen right outside his shop, so grab your target a few blocks down the road. Once inside his bay, you’ll have to apply a fresh respray before the registration option unlocks. And make sure you have an open garage slot ready if you plan to expand beyond your first free claim.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.title_zh: SpaceX’s subsidiary Cursor tells lawmakers it's considering phasing out Chinese AI models
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX's artificial-intelligence coding platform, Cursor, is considering moving away from using of Chinese AI models due to "geopolitical risk," CNBC has learned.
Cursor, which SpaceX acquired at an implied $60 billion equity value in August, had built its coding model Composer 2 on top of Chinese lab Moonshot AI's Kimi K2.5.
It's among the U.S. firms that have adopted Chinese models, whose usage has spiked across the globe this year, worrying lawmakers in Washington . The battle for AI supremacy between the U.S. and China has reached new heights in 2026 as Chinese models have improved.
But now Cursor plans to "explore phasing out PRC [People's Republic of China]-developed open-weight models because of geopolitical risk," according to a report produced by the House Committee on Homeland Security and the House Select Committee on China, shared exclusively with CNBC ahead of its publication on Friday.
The report, which follows a months-long investigation into the adoption of Chinese AI models into the American tech stack, said Cursor "informed the Committees" of those plans. Airbnb and DoorDash also engaged with the investigation about their use of Chinese AI models.
SpaceX announced it entered into a formal agreement to buy Cursor in June; the deal was completed in August. SpaceX is developing the Grok family of models, which Cursor has been involved in training.
Cursor, SpaceX and DoorDash did not respond to a CNBC request for comment. Airbnb declined to comment. The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
The report found that cost, customization and near-frontier performance of Chinese AI models were driving adoption, with the U.S. lacking a competitive open-weight alternative at "price and performance the market demands."
"Beijing is now seeking to turn those technological gains into global market share and long-term dependence," the report says. China's embassy in the U.K. did not respond to a request for comment. China's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond.
It also sets out recommendations to address the issues it has identified.
Those include launching a "national American open-weight initiative" that combines public computing power, shared evaluation infrastructure and "lawful access" to American frontier models for training.
The report also says an order, made public in October, that banned DeepSeek from federal civilian agency systems, should be built on, by prohibiting the use of "PRC-developed AI models" in federal information systems and in performance of federal contracts.
Separately, Washington is also concerned about Chinese companies accessing Nvidia chips remotely , via overseas data centers, and gaining ground by using " distillation ," where new models use older, more established ones to help train them.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.

articles.title_orig: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
articles.title_zh: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
articles.content_orig:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way cases are defended in court.
Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period , using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.
The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials.
Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"
Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse
Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers without her knowledge.
During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.
The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.
The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".
There is no defined law which states third-party consent is a valid defence.
In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone... and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.
"This is simply unacceptable."
Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial.
"No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.
"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."
Kate Parker, criminal barrister and founder of the Schools Consent Project, said legally, a third party or a partner cannot consent on a person's behalf.
"The law makes that very clear. A person consents if he or she agrees by choice and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice," she added.
"In a case like this where someone has been made unconscious, there is no possible way that that person is able to consent because of course they have no capacity."
She added that the defendants' claims that they thought Joanne Young had consented through her husband "doesn't make sense legally, and that's not a legal position that can be supported in court".
Parker said the defence used by the four men in the trial is not a correct application of the law but might be something defence lawyers would try and rely on as their client's genuine belief in their victim's consent, or in mitigation to try and get a lower sentence.
Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life.
"It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said.
"You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."
Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations.
"The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked.
"So why are they still accessible?" she said.
Bishop understands why many choose to maintain their anonymity but wants to encourage those who can speak out to do so.
"There's a million reasons why its not be appropriate to waive your anonymity and it might just be because it's something you can't actively do," she said.
"But for those of us that are able to, we have to stand strong for victims."
Debbie Beadle, chief executive officer at Wiltshire-based domestic abuse charity Fear Free, also hopes that Joanne Young's decision to speak out will encourage others to do so.
"Six in seven rapes against women are done by someone they know and this adds a barrier to people coming forward," she said.
"The fact that Joanne has come forward will help others when this has happened to them."
Zoe Watts is the founder of a global campaign called End Eye Check that works to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse.
Like Joanne Young and Bishop, Watts waived her right to anonymity after she was drugged and raped by her husband.
Watts hopes that Joanne Young's case "sets a precedent", but told Woman's Hour that the crime is more widespread than many realise.
"I have had women contact me from 25 different countries," she said.
"It's a daily process of women either contacting me because they've woken up to find their husband having sex with them while they're asleep and have done on numerous occasions.
"Or perhaps they're not sure if they've been drugged or maybe they are genuinely asleep and wake up and find him that way, or women that have found videos or recordings on their phone of things they haven't consented to," Watts added.
Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC that more needs to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators.
"The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said.
"We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments.
"[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."
Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told Radio 4's Woman's Hour that current laws do not do enough to protect women.
"The law says that somebody can seek a defence to defend themselves against a rape claim if they reasonably believe that they had consent," said Phillips.
"These people went on to argue that they reasonably believed that Joanne's husband had sought her consent and got it.
"They were found guilty, but it's whether the law needs to explicitly say, 'you cannot reasonably believe someone's given consent unless they have given it'.
"If there was clarity in the law, Joanne wouldn't have been put through the court case," Phillips added.
She also believes that more needs to be done to hold the websites hosting adverts and similar content to account.
"Can every pornographic site in our country categorically say that not one of these snuff videos or sedated videos is on their site?
"Unless they can guarantee it with a signed piece of paper from the person that they know is in that video [they should not be published]," Phillips said.

articles.title_orig: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.title_zh: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.content_orig:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting, who was visiting Poland on Friday, said: "The impact of Russia's illegal war is being felt across Ukraine and increasingly in neighbouring countries." Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Friday's incident was "utterly unacceptable".
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title_orig: Estonia to close border with Russia, Moscow decries 'new Iron Curtain'
articles.title_zh: Estonia to close border with Russia, Moscow decries 'new Iron Curtain'
articles.content_orig:
Authorities say Russian intelligence service ordered attack which Estonian PM links to Tallinn’s support for Ukraine
Estonia will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after a suspected sabotage attack on a drone maker in the Baltic state over the weekend, which authorities said was ordered by Russia’s GRU military intelligence service.
On Saturday morning, eight people were detained during an attempted attack on Threod Systems, a defence company that manufactures long-range attack and reconnaissance drones. No injuries or damage were reported after the company’s security team responded to the incident.
Estonia’s internal security service, Kapo, said on Sunday the attack was carried out “with the aim of causing an explosion and setting the building on fire”. Authorities have requested a court order for five of those detained to remain in custody, Estonia’s public broadcaster ERR reported.
The Estonian prime minister, Kristen Michal, said the border closure was needed to reduce the risk of further attacks and “send a clear message that attacks on Estonia’s defence industry and defence capabilities” were unacceptable.
He linked the attacks with Estonia’s continuing support for Ukraine . “Russia’s aim is to make us afraid, make us hesitate and weaken our support for Ukraine,” Michal said.
“Estonia’s response is the opposite. We will strengthen our security, work even more closely with businesses and our allies, increase pressure on Russia and continue supporting Ukraine.”
The Estonian foreign minister, Margus Tsahkna, echoed the warning, saying : “Russia must understand that hostile actions against Estonia come with consequences. Attempts to intimidate, destabilise or undermine our security will not go unanswered.”
Estonia operates three border crossings with Russia – Narva in the north, and Koidula and Luhamaa in the south. The authorities did not specify how long the closure would be.
It is the second attempted attack on an Estonian defence company that authorities have attributed to Russia, after an arson attack at Milrem Robotics in August.
In September, Kapo said it was confident that the incident was “a deliberate and pre-planned attack carried out on behalf of Russian special services”.
The agency also said it fitted a pattern of Russian attacks targeting defence and drone companies, particularly those with links to Ukraine.
At the time Estonia summoned Russia’s chargé d’affaires over the attack, but the Kremlin denied any link to Russia, saying it was a “baseless” and “ill-considered” accusation “with absolutely no relation to reality”.
Several European intelligence services have repeatedly warned of potential attacks on defence companies and growing Russian attempts to recruit citizens in EU and Nato countries – on online messaging platforms – to carry out acts of sabotage.
Michal noted that the weekend’s arrests came after security agencies told the defence industry of potential risks. “We do not warn about these threats without reason. Preparedness matters, and this time it clearly paid off,” he said.
The Russian foreign ministry spokesperson, Maria Zakharova, told state news agency Tass: “If ‌these [border closures] are ‌their real plans, then ‌they fit into yet another bout of aggressive and unrestrained Russophobia.”

articles.title_orig: iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more
articles.title_zh: iOS 27.3: New features, release date, more
articles.content_orig:
One of iPhone Duo 's biggest disadvantages is the lack of Face ID. Apple 's convenient way of unlocking the phone just by presenting your face simply did not fit on the thin foldable device, so Apple went with Touch ID on the power button instead.
But Touch ID, as quick as it is, is just a tad more of a hassle than simply picking the Duo up and having it unlock with a glance. Luckily, Apple figured out a way to fix this.
In the latest developer beta of iOS 27.3, the Duo has a new option, located under Settings - Touch ID & Passcode, called "Unlock with Front Camera." Turn it on, go through a quick onboarding process (similar to the one you do with the regular Face Unlock on other iPhones), and you'll be able to unlock the foldable just by looking at its front screen.
I've tried it out on my Duo, and it works as expected, easily unlocking the phone every time, even when my face was a little off to the side. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile
There are caveats here, though. Face ID includes a 3D scanning mechanism making it a lot more secure, while this new feature on the Duo uses the front camera alone for face recognition. This is why Apple put a few additional safeguards in place. First, this system only works for unlocking the phone; for Apple Pay or accessing your password, you'll still need to use Touch ID. Also, face unlock won't work after 45 minutes of inactivity; you'll have to use Touch ID or passcode after that much time has passed. Finally, the system only works on the outer display, which has a better camera. Unlocking the phone via the FaceTime camera on the inner display will not work.
Apple's own warning below the option in the settings confirms this. "Use the front camera, along with a recent Touch ID or passcode authentication, to quickly unlock iPhone Duo when it's closed. Face recognition data never leaves your device. To use Apple Pay or to access your password, Touch ID is still required."
If you don't mind the weakened security, this is a pretty handy option, even given its limitations. I've already set up to unlock the iPhone Duo with my Apple Watch Ultra , so this doesn't change much, but users who don't have the Watch or don't wear it all the time might appreciate the face unlock feature.

articles.title_zh: U.S.-China trade, Taiwan and tech tensions remain unresolved as Trump returns from Asia
articles.content_orig:
China's Xi Jinping, US President Donald Trump and Russia's Vladimir Putin are pictured together in Shenzhen for the first time - images show the leaders shaking hands
They're together for the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit. Earlier, Xi welcomed Trump with a hug on the tarmac - a carefully choreographed moment of flattery, writes our correspondent
The pair will have historic trilateral talks with Putin on Thursday - Xi has called the Russian leader an "old friend"
Our Russia editor says some newspapers are already calling this visit a "diplomatic victory" for Putin - simply because it's happening
Meanwhile, Trump arrives from the Philippines where he attended another summit - here's a recap of the trip so far
Edited by Manish Pandey, with Laura Bicker, Steve Rosenberg and Stephen McDonell in China and Nada Tawfik travelling with President Trump
Malu Cursino Live reporter
China President Xi Jinping, Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump made headlines a day before their trilateral talks, as the group of influential world leaders were pictured together in Shenzhen for the Apec summit.
Trump's visit comes as his top team wrestles with how to handle China in the wake of a recent alleged spying scandal that has engulfed tech firm Nvidia, as our North America reporter explains .
While focus is on the three superpowers - China, Russia and the US - Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney arrived in Asia in the days leading up to the Apec summit, hoping to make deals to reduce his country's reliance on the US.
Despite the warm welcome shown to Trump, China and Russia were united in their criticism of US economic sanctions and restrictions. In Russia meanwhile, Kremlin-backed media called the Trump-Putin handshake in the presence of Xi "historic" .
Anthony Zurcher North America correspondent
This is the kind of high-profile diplomatic event Donald Trump just loves. The American president, standing alongside the leaders of China and Russia, to tackle issues of global importance.
Although Thursday's trilateral meeting was reportedly the idea of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Trump - whose political worldview was formed during the high-stakes drama of the Cold War â has seemed to be an enthusiastic participant.
It fits with Trumpâs push to reorient American foreign policy into old-fashioned spheres of influence, where the mighty sit down to make the rules for the rest of us.
Itâs not clear what the purpose of the specific gathering might be, beyond the optics. Trump appears keen to discuss nuclear disarmament â another Cold War artifact, perhaps.
The growing power of artificial intelligence, which could be the more pressing, perhaps even existential, threat to global security and economic prosperity isnât likely to come up here or in separate bilateral talks with Chinese leader Xi Jinping in any substantive way.
It has been an eventful Wednesday, as China hosts this year's Apec summit in Shenzhen - the country's AI capital.
On the sidelines of the summit tomorrow, President Xi Jinping will host trilateral talks with Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin.
Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr hosted Trump at MalacaÃ±ang Palace for lunch on Wednesday, before the US president left for China
Xi met Trump on the tarmac, marking a rare break from his longstanding tradition of not greeting other leaders off plane
A senior Beijing official - not Xi - met Putin as he stepped off the plane in the early hours in Shenzhen. Russian and Chinese delegations held talks later on Wednesday
Putin and Xi held a meeting on the sidelines of the summit
Liza Fokht BBC News Russian
Russian media are describing the meeting between Xi, Putin and Trump in Shenzhen (which we have just seen) as "the main images of the day". One state news agency called the scene a "historic handshake".
This is precisely the image the Kremlin was hoping for.
Unlike the US and China, Russia is not among the world's three largest economies. Yet at the Apec summit, Vladimir Putin clearly feels like a leader equal to Xi and Trump.
Moscow is sending a message to the world: attempts to isolate Russia have failed, despite its ongoing war in Ukraine.
And while tomorrow's meeting between the leaders is unlikely to produce any practical results, Putin has already achieved his main objective.
His very presence in this club, and the attention of the world's media, allows Moscow to position itself as one of the world's unshakable powers.
James FitzGerald North America reporter
This visit to China by US President Donald Trump comes as his top team wrestle with how to handle China in the wake of a recent alleged spying scandal that has engulfed American tech firm Nvidia.
It has unfolded against the backdrop of a fierce AI race - in which the US and China are the world's top two competitors. Nvidia is central to Trump's mission to dominate in the field.
The president himself has acknowledged that he has competing voices in his ear when it comes to dealing Beijing.
Last week, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed Howard Lutnick's Commerce Department for failing to properly oversee the export of US-made chips - a key part of AI tech.
Both men have accompanied Trump for his visit to Asia. Asked about the two men's relationship before setting off, Trump responded: "They're fine. They have two different views."
He added: "One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blow-up with China."
Howard Lutnick (left) and Scott Bessent (centre) have differing views
The US administration has taken relatively tough steps over the issue in recent days, indicating that the figures who take a hawkish stance to China are proving influential.
For one, the US has confirmed it is investigating a Singapore-based company which is suspected of breaking US restrictions by helping Nvidia's chips to China.
The Trump administration also renewed its efforts to further curb China's access to advanced semiconductors - which are also critical for the AI industry.
We've just received the "family photo" of the leaders of economies in the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec).
Front and centre is China's President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan. US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin are also in the front row - with Trump next to Xi.
Other leaders, including Canada's Mark Carney and Japan's Sanae Takaichi are in the second row.
Jack Lau Global China Unit, reporting from Hong Kong
President Xi Jinping may have given President Donald Trump a rare personal welcome at Shenzhen airport, but he joins President Vladimir Putin in sharply criticising US economic sanctions and restrictions.
At the Apec CEO summit this morning, Xi called for "free and open trade", while Putin touted Russia's resilience under sanctions.
Russia's military, technology and industrial sectors have been targeted over Moscow's war in Ukraine. China, meanwhile, faces sanctions and restrictions linked to human rights, advanced technology and military development.
Xi has repeatedly criticised sanctions from Washington DC, here at Apec and elsewhere. Beijing says it does not recognise unilateral sanctions imposed outside the UN Security Council, where China and Russia both hold veto powers.
Dr Wan Qingsong, a Russia expert in Shanghai, says both countries are facing growing pressures as supply chains fragment and governments move to protect domestic industries, particularly hi-tech sectors.
"For China and Russia, working more closely together is not only about mutual economic benefit - it is also a way to guard against global economic risks," says Wan, also the deputy director of East China Normal University's Russia Studies Centre.
Nada Tawfik North America correspondent, travelling with President Trump
This has been a fast-paced trip to Asia for the US President.
Itâs clear from his various engagements that heâs been relishing the warm reception heâs received from Manila to Shenzhen.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
articles.title_zh: Anthropic raises $93.5 billion total as underwriters scoop up ‘greenshoe’ overallotment
articles.content_orig:
Anthropic underwriters have officially exercised their overallotment of shares in the historic initial public offering , bringing the total raised to $93.5 billion, according to a release Friday.
The artificial intelligence company raised $81.3 billion on Wednesday and netted an additional $12.2 billion through the overallotment, surpassing SpaceX , which held a record IPO in June.
Anthropic said it sold an aggregate of 1,127,000,000 shares of its Class A common stock at $83 per share in the offering. It sold 980 million shares on Wednesday and its underwriters had the option to purchase up to an additional 147 million shares by Friday as part of the overallotment, which is commonly referred to as the "greenshoe."
Shares of the Claude maker opened trading at $111.50 on the Nasdaq on Thursday, but slid throughout the day and closed at $97.17. The stock sank 12% in premarket trading on Friday during a broad tech sell-off.
In addition to the sale of its Class A common stock, Anthropic closed a concurrent sale of its Class N common stock after a group of tech companies, including Advanced Micro Devices , Google , Microsoft , Nvidia and others, agreed to participate in a $26 billion private placement at the IPO price. Anthropic said Friday that aggregate gross proceeds from its IPO, including the private placement, totaled $119.5 billion, before deducting offering expenses.
Anthropic dodged an unforgiving series of obstacles on its road to the Nasdaq on Thursday, as investors brooded over Jensen Huang's shocking ouster at Nvidia, voters' stinging rebuke of the tech during the midterms and whether rising interest rates would stymie industry plans for a multitrillion-dollar AI infrastructure buildout .
CEO Dario Amodei co-founded the company in 2021 after he and a handful of other researchers, including his sister Daniela, quit their jobs at OpenAI , now Anthropic's chief rival. Anthropic is best known for developing a family of AI models called Claude , which have captivated the corporate world and fueled the company's historic rise.
The siblings celebrated the IPO as a "milestone" in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, but said there's more work ahead for Anthropic.
"For us, it's like one stop on the journey," Daniela Amodei said. "We think about this as, 'Wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company.'"

articles.title_orig: The Morning Risk Report: China’s AI Firms Are Hooked on Nvidia Chips. Now Comes the Withdrawal.
articles.title_zh: The Morning Risk Report: China’s AI Firms Are Hooked on Nvidia Chips. Now Comes the Withdrawal.
articles.content_orig:
The subagency of the Commerce Department that regulates and enforces exports approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies including Alibaba and Tencent as of May 2026, according to documents released Thursday by the House Foreign Affairs Committee.
Some of those approvals, made by Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, included sales to companies designated by the Department of Defense as "Chinese Military Companies," according to the documents. From December through May, companies had made 3.4 million requests for sales of U.S. AI chips to China, the committee reported, citing those made by Nvidia and Advanced Micro Devices .
"Over the past month, the administration's handling of chip export controls has put our national security and technology edge at risk. The Bureau of Industry and Security has failed to enforce the rules, and Congress must now conduct rigorous oversight of the administration's policies," Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, said at a meeting of the panel Thursday at which members voted to release the documents.
Spokespersons for Nvidia and AMD said their companies comply with U.S. export control laws.
Nvidia argued it was following the Commerce Department regulations that were in effect at the time.
A spokesperson from the Bureau of Industry and Security said it shared information with Congress on both approvals and denials of licenses for Nvidia's H200 and comparable chips. "Licensing decisions are the product of deliberation and consultation among multiple U.S. Government agencies," the spokesperson said.
"The review and licensing process spanned more than half a year, with approvals subject to strict conditions and limited volumes. Despite receiving some licenses, we have since stopped shipping H200s to China," Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo told CNBC.
On Tuesday, Nvidia reported $2.4 billion in quarterly revenue from H200 and related chip sales in China. In total, customers based in China and Hong Kong made up about 9.5% of all revenue.
"AMD complies with applicable U.S. export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations," AMD said through a spokesperson.
The approval of 879,000 AI chips is "not that many," Bernstein Senior Analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC, adding that this news is not surprising.
"It doesn't sound to me like they're approving everything they got willy nilly," Rasgon said of the Commerce Department. With 879,000 approvals out of 3.4 million requested AI chip sales, he added, "There was a process in place, and it sounds like they approved about one out of every four."
Despite a rapid succession of China export controls on AI chips that started under the Biden administration in 2022, Nvidia and AMD both re-engineered some chips to comply and be sold legally in China. And in December, Trump said Nvidia could ship H200s, its older generation Hopper chips, to "approved customers in China" if the U.S. got a 25% cut of sales.
The U.S. then licensed Nvidia H200 sales to Alibaba , Tencent, ByteDance and other Chinese companies, although sales were limited because Beijing didn't approve large-scale imports, chip analyst Patrick Moorhead of Moor Insights & Strategy told CNBC last week.
H200 sales numbers remained low due to those restrictions on China's end. Nvidia said H200 shipments to China made up less than 1% of data center revenue for the quarter that ended in July.
"In the grand context of the size of this market and how much they're shipping, it's a rounding error. It's tiny," Rasgon told CNBC.
The committee cited the Export Control Reform Act as justification for releasing the data. The panel said the law allows it to declassify and release export data if it "determines that the withholding of the following information is contrary to the national interest."
The license requests released by the Foreign Affairs Committee include requests to sell to major firms including ByteDance, Tesla (Shanghai) and Baidu .
The release of documents comes in the wake of Jensen Huang 's resignation from the chip supplier Nvidia after news surfaced that he had several extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese spy that led to concerns about Nvidia chips being diverted to China.
In the weeks since, Republicans and Democrats in Congress have called for legislation to be passed that would impose stricter export controls on the sale of advanced AI chips to China and other adversaries.
"The license information we are disclosing today will help inform the American public about how BIS has handled licenses for Nvidia H200 and equivalent AMD chips to China. The public has the right to know how these decisions were made," Meeks said.
Mast said two of the firms listed in Nvidia license applications to BIS —  Maginfra and New Matrix — are suspected "smuggling fronts." The New York Times reported in November that both companies had empty offices and had ties to companies under national security sanctions.
"Both are fake companies. If BIS approved the sale of these chips to these firms, obviously that is of tremendous concern to us — especially given that President Trump made clear last year that the sale of any AI chips to China will have very real national security conditions," Mast said at the Thursday meeting.
Maginfra and New Matrix did not reply to requests for comment.
Shares of AMD fell Thursday after the investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging the company "has its own China problem." The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Fallout from the Huang scandal on Capitol Hill has intensified in the last week, as lawmakers question the degree to which the former head of Nvidia's relationship with the suspected Chinese spy could have jeopardized national security and American AI dominance.
Huang is due for a closed-door transcribed interview with the House Foreign Affairs panel and two other committees on Dec. 1. Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter is scheduled to appear before the panels Dec. 2.
Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., announced on CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had also agreed to testify.
Lutnick has come under fire over his relationship to Huang and for his failure to take action on Megaspeed , the Singaporean company where Alice Huang , with whom the former Nvidia CEO had an affair, was an executive until 2025. U.S. investigators suspect Megaspeed diverted Nvidia chips to China.
Amid that criticism, the Commerce Department on Monday issued an interim final rule to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia's advancing computing power from data centers in third countries.
The rule was "written by and at the direction of" the Treasury Department and the White House National Security Council, BIS said in a press release.
— Megan Cassella , Daren Fonda and Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
articles.title_zh: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
articles.content_orig:
Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’
Signal will now restrict screenshots on mobile devices, and says AI agents are ‘hostile to privacy.’
Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post , while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.
“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”
Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri , Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system.
Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.
“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

articles.content_orig:

Donald Trump ’s top foreign envoys have suggested that Ukraine could still join the Nato military alliance in closed-door talks over the past few months, according to a shocking new report.
The idea of granting Ukraine membership to the bloc has long been considered dead in the water , a red line for a Russia that has opposed even the idea of deploying Nato peacekeepers in a post-war settlement.
But sources familiar with the matter told the Wall Street Journal that Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has suggested that Kyiv could still join if it bends to Moscow ’s central demand for it to give up territory.
They said he had recently taken the idea right to Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky and other European officials in an effort to break the deadlock in peace talks.
The idea apparently emerged in August, some six months after a round of talks in Geneva ended without any clear breakthroughs.
It since came up at a meeting with both sides in the UAE, although it was unclear from the report what the Kremlin had made of it.
Ukraine maintains that it cannot and will not give up control of its eastern lands, which are mineral rich and host its defensive line of ‘fortress cities’ - as well as thousands of Ukrainian citizens.
But Nato membership could go some way to ensuring Ukraine gets its desired security guarantees against a future invasion.
The US, Russia and the UK offered security assurances when Ukraine gave up its nuclear weapons in 1994, but those failed to stop Vladimir Putin annexing Crimea in 2014 and launching a full-scale invasion in 2022.
And Trump has since cast doubt on whether he would even help a Nato ally in the event of an attack, saying last year he would not defend countries that failed to meet his “requirements” on defence spending.
In 2024, before his second term, he drew criticism for saying he would “encourage” Russia to attack any Nato member that fails to pay its bills.
An attack on Nato without the US - the bloc’s largest contributor - would leave Europe and Canada a weakened force against any potential adversary.
The growing rift between Washington and Europe since Trump’s return to office was felt this week as he met Putin on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Shenzhen , China.
Trump greeted the Russian leader by asking “Who is he? He’s my friend” before the two settled into discussions on the Ukraine war.
It was later reported that Trump reportedly had urged Europe to stop funding Ukraine, just hours after the warm bilateral with Putin.
Trump was said to have called into a meeting with the so-called Coalition of the Willing in Germany, attended by UK prime minister Andy Burnham and Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelensky, among others.
He raised concerns about billions in aid provided to Ukraine from Europe, according to European officials in Politico and Telegraph reports , stressing countries could save money if the war ended.
An unnamed US official later told Politico it was “not accurate” to say Trump told the leaders to end funding to Kyiv, but rather repeated his desire to bring the conflict to an end.

articles.title_orig: Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’
articles.title_zh: Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’
articles.content_orig:
Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.
Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.
"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's " Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.
Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.
"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."
The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.
In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF , Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX , representing more than 21% of the fund together.
Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.
The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.
Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.
"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

articles.title_orig: Stocks slide despite Anthropic’s record debut and Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ China summit: Morning Rundown
articles.title_zh: Stocks slide despite Anthropic’s record debut and Trump touts ‘unbelievable’ China summit: Morning Rundown
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine , is wanted by the International Criminal Court on allegations of war crimes , and is accused of overseeing a yearslong campaign of election interference, sabotage and cyberattacks against the West.
So when President Donald Trump pointed to the Russian leader and declared, “He’s my friend,” at the historic Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China on Thursday, the reaction from some of America’s closest European allies was one of alarm and disbelief.
“God, protect us from such friends,” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk posted to X shortly afterward.
“The optics of embracing Putin and calling him a friend cause us some concern,” Poland’s foreign minister, Radosław Sikorski, told a news conference Thursday. He added that it posed the question of whom Trump considered a closer friend, Putin or Poland, and “if push came to shove, which friend would he choose?”
Their comments came hours before Poland’s defense minister, Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz, accused Russia of violating the country’s airspace overnight with three objects that were probably two missiles and a drone. Elsewhere, Estonia said it would close its road border crossings with Russia on security grounds for at least six months.
Much of the criticism of Trump’s remark has come from Poland, historically one of Washington’s closest allies in Europe but whose officials have grown increasingly wary of Trump’s dealings with Russia . The country, which borders Ukraine, Russia and Moscow’s close ally Belarus, has long been among the most outspoken European governments warning about the threat of Russian aggression. Its security strategy also relies heavily on the United States and NATO.
More broadly, the word “friend” also caused fresh alarm among other European governments, some of which are openly warning that Putin may expand his aggression beyond Ukraine and attack them, too.
Ultimately, there is widespread concern that elevating Putin alongside Trump and China’s Xi Jinping will legitimize and embolden a leader whom Western governments have sought to isolate over his record of grave human rights abuses and aggression against other countries, allegations he has routinely denied.
The joint declaration made by Trump, Putin and Xi after their meeting made no mention of Ukraine but condemned the International Criminal Court , which has issued a warrant for Putin’s arrest over the alleged unlawful deportation of Ukrainian children to Russia.
Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said it was “very incomprehensible” that Trump would meet with Putin, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz was among those who warned against the meeting becoming a rerun of the Yalta Conference of 1945 . The summit toward the end of World War II saw President Franklin D. Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin effectively carve up occupied Germany and other parts of Europe.
Others, including British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, were more restrained. Asked whether Trump had “fallen for Putin’s charm offensive,” he replied that it was “quite the opposite” and that Trump had “talked about the horrific loss of life, including the loss of young Russian lives, and he spoke quite passionately about that subject.”
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte also defended the principle of nuclear powers meeting to pursue diplomacy.
Burnham and Rutte were speaking at a meeting in Berlin of the “Coalition of the Willing,” a group of nearly 40 countries working to support Ukraine and provide security guarantees.
They were joined by Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, the U.S. envoys tasked with brokering peace between Moscow and Kyiv.
Trump called into a meeting of dozens of European leaders and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Thursday, telling the group that Putin was ready to end the war, according to five European officials briefed on the discussions. He also encouraged the Europeans to make a deal so they can stop spending money on Ukraine and spend it on their own countries, the officials said.
Kushner also mentioned the call in a post on X but said it was up to the president to reveal what he said.
“Trump wants to make a deal with Europe by his side. He’s not looking to impose anything unilaterally,” Kushner said. “Any deal we do will be in close consultation with Ukraine and with Europe. That’s something that he also asked us to come here today and reassure people in that regard.”
The White House did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment on the criticisms about Trump’s comment about Putin. But Trump defended his description of the Russian president in an interview with Reuters, saying that “it’s nice to have people that have 4,000 nuclear weapons as a friend as opposed to an enemy.”
This is far from the first time Trump has spoken warmly about Putin, joking in 2013 about becoming his “new best friend.” Once in office, Trump said in 2018 that the pair “got on very well,” and in 2022, he described Putin’s initial moves against Ukraine as “genius” and “savvy.” In 2023 and again in 2024, Trump recounted telling Putin, “We’re friends.”
However, this week was the first time Trump made the declaration to Putin’s face, in front of television cameras at one of the most hotly anticipated meetings of recent years.
“It’s one thing to say in an interview, ‘We get on,’ as Trump has in the past; it’s quite another to see him crossing a room in the hotel in China with an effusive smile on his face and gushing about ‘my friend,’” said Jonathan Eyal, international director of the Royal United Services Institute, a London-based think tank. “It all felt very natural and very real.”
The condemnation was not confined to one side of the Atlantic.
In the United States, Democrats were openly scathing. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York called Trump’s words “embarrassing, despicable, and quite frankly pathetic,” while Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, described Trump’s “friend” as a “murderous war criminal.”
Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona said: “Putin is not my friend. He’s not your friend. He’s not a friend of this country, and when the president of the United States refers to him in that way, it emboldens him.”
Republicans were more circumspect. Sen. Rick Scott of Florida called Putin a “thug” but acknowledged that Trump needed to work with him.
Bill Browder, a British American financier who spearheaded the international campaign for Russian sanctions and has become one of Putin’s most prominent critics, also described his “revulsion and disgust” at hearing Trump’s words.
“He’s a guy who’s a geopolitical menace, and he should not get any kind of respect, let alone from the American head of state,” Browder told NBC News in a telephone interview. “To be elevated to the top table with genuine superpowers is an unbelievable symbolic position to sit in.”
When asked about Trump’s comment at the end of the news conference following the “Coalition of the Willing” meeting in the German capital, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy only shrugged and walked offstage.
Alexander Smith is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital based in London.
Abigail Williams is a producer and reporter for NBC News covering the State Department.

articles.title_orig: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes
articles.title_zh: Rejecting cheap fabrics, higher prices: Why shoppers are asking for better clothes
articles.content_orig:
US shoppers are paying closer attention to clothing labels as prices reach record highs, according to AlixPartners. Imported garments made mostly from synthetic fibers have become more common than cotton, while brands emphasizing natural materials have seen signs of demand.
US shoppers are rejecting cheap fabrics sold at higher prices, according to an AlixPartners survey of more than 9,000 consumers. The findings come as apparel prices reach record highs and synthetic fibers make up most clothing imports.
Clothing prices generally fell over the two decades before the pandemic, according to the consumer price index. They have risen to record highs since 2020.
Shoppers are checking labels more closely as they weigh whether garments are worth their price, the consulting firm's 2026 Consumer Sentiment Index found. Many are also paying more for food, gas, rent and other essentials.
About 60% of clothing imported into the US in 2010 was predominantly cotton. That share is now around 45%, while garments made mostly from synthetic fibers such as polyester and nylon account for the majority.
Fast fashion, the growth of athletic-inspired clothing and changes to supply chains helped drive the shift. Inexpensive synthetic fabrics also helped brands produce new garments faster and at lower prices.
US Commerce Department data show that synthetic garments imported between January and August 2026 cost an average of $2.64 per square meter. Mostly cotton garments cost $3.67 per square meter.
Those are import costs, not the prices shoppers pay in stores. Compared with 2010, synthetic apparel import costs rose around 11%, while cotton apparel costs increased 21%.
Polyester can help clothes hold their shape and draw sweat away from the body. Research has also raised concerns that washing polyester clothing can release microplastics.
Bernstein Research senior retail analyst Aneesha Sherman said the growth of athletic-inspired clothing was a major factor in polyester's rise. Euromonitor data showed US sports apparel grew at a 4.9% rate from 2015 to 2025, against 2.6% for all apparel and footwear.
Ralph Lauren said around 90% of its apparel is primarily made from cotton, leather, wool, viscose, cashmere or silk, according to its 2026 sustainability report. The company sold more products at full price and reduced markdowns in fiscal 2026.
Ralph Lauren's stock has risen around 85% over the past two years. Quince, a direct-to-consumer clothing brand focused on natural materials, reached a $10 billion valuation in 2026.
Some fast-fashion brands lost ground in the AlixPartners survey. Shein and Zara each fell three places in the young adult specialty category, to fifth and seventh respectively.
Shein passed higher tariff costs on to shoppers in 2025 and blamed a sales slowdown on the higher prices. Zara has continued to grow sales and profits year over year despite its lower survey ranking.
AlixPartners head of fashion Sonia Lapinsky said consumer sentiment can sometimes signal future changes. “I'm not saying that this is going to be true for Zara,” she said, adding that the firm would watch the brand in upcoming quarters and into 2027.

articles.title_orig: Deadly Russian strikes hit 3 Kyiv bridges after Putin vows revenge for Crimea attacks
articles.title_zh: Deadly Russian strikes hit 3 Kyiv bridges after Putin vows revenge for Crimea attacks
articles.content_orig:
KYIV, Ukraine — Three bridges in Kyiv were hit Friday in a massive Russian ballistic missile attack, officials in the Ukrainian capital said, hours after President Vladimir Putin vowed “painful” revenge for strikes on his prized bridge linking Crimea to Russia .
The attacks, which started in the early hours of the morning and continued well into the day, damaged the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi, Darnytskyi and Southern bridges connecting the left and right banks of the Dnipro River, which flows through the city, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a post on Telegram.
At least six people were killed and 15 injured in those strikes, Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said in a separate post. Two others were killed in separate attacks across the country, which saw nine regions hit overnight, he said.
The strikes on Kyiv forced authorities to restrict traffic on the bridges, impacting the movement across the capital. Klitschko asked residents not to drive private cars into the city “unless absolutely necessary” and suggested employers let staff work remotely.
Russia has been hitting Kyiv’s Southern and Northern bridges since early October, causing multiple closures, disrupting metro services and causing traffic jams.
But it is the first time that Russia hit three different bridges in a single night, and it has left most of the main road crossings over the Dnipro simultaneously damaged or restricted.
An NBC News team in Kyiv heard air raid sirens going off every few minutes overnight, accompanied by loud explosions.
After dawn broke on the rainy and foggy Friday morning, firefighters were seen putting out the flames from a strike on an industrial area in the capital.
It’s part of the daily reality for Kyiv’s residents after Russia escalated both the number of ballistic missiles it was firing at the capital and the frequency of attacks.
The latest strikes came hours after Putin said that Moscow would retaliate after Ukraine struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia and Crimea for a third time this week .
Speaking in the Chinese city of Shenzhen after his much-touted trilateral meeting with President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, Putin said Moscow would hit back hard for the attacks on his flagship project. The Kerch Bridge was meant to solidify Russian dominance over Crimea, the peninsula he illegally annexed in 2014.
“We will respond to these strikes. I want everyone to know that,” Putin told reporters, adding that Russia’s response will be “far more painful” than what Kyiv did to the Kerch Bridge, which cost billions of dollars to build.
Putin personally opened the road and rail bridge, which is the longest in Europe, in 2018. Beyond its symbolic value, the bridge has served as a vital supply route for the Russian military and civilians in Crimea.
Putin insisted Thursday that the bridge was “an exclusively civilian facility,” but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has called it “the main military crossing from Russian territory into our Ukrainian Crimea.”
On Friday, Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said that Russia’s attempts to justify its attacks as “responses” to any of his country’s own attacks should be unacceptable.
“Putting Russia and Ukraine on an equal footing is fundamentally wrong,” he said, adding: “This week, Putin posed for photographs with world leaders. But the photograph he deserves is one of him in the dock, where he stands trial for crimes against Ukrainians and Ukraine.”
Acknowledging Friday’s strikes on Kyiv’s bridges, Russia said they were used for military purposes — the line of reasoning Moscow has used in the past to justify bridge attacks in Kyiv.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s air force said Friday that Russia used ballistic and cruise missiles, as well as more than 400 drones, in the massive attack against 23 locations across the country.
Zelenskyy said 27 of over 110 missiles launched at Ukraine overnight were ballistic. Nearly 80 cruise missiles were shot down, he said. “Ballistic missiles are, unfortunately, much more difficult to deal with, and that depends not on our capabilities but on the supply of missiles by our partners,” he added.
Zelenskyy told NBC News in an interview on Wednesday that Ukraine was experiencing a “deficit” of American-made Patriot interceptor missiles that can stop Russian ballistic strikes, with U.S. deliveries falling this year. This was posing “a huge problem and challenge” for Kyiv, he said.
The country’s energy authorities also said Russian strikes on power plants and substations, which have been ongoing since early fall, left people in Kyiv and 10 other regions without power.
Richard Engel and Michael Fiorentino reported from Kyiv. Yuliya Talmazan reported from London.
NBC News Chief Foreign Correspondent
Michael Fiorentino is a London-based producer for NBC News.
Yuliya Talmazan is a reporter for NBC News Digital, based in London.
